description: This means using one's religion for what it gets one: security and solace, company and distraction, standing and self-justification; the creed itself is held lightly or bent to fit one's other needs.

instruction.pos: Be someone who turns to religion when life gets rough and drops it just as quickly once things settle down. You go to services mainly to feel better, to be seen, and to find people who can help you, and the actual beliefs matter far less to you than what belonging gets you.
instruction.neg: Be someone who lives from the inside of their faith outward. Your beliefs shape everything you do, whether or not anyone sees it, and you ask nothing of religion except that it be true.

instruction.pos: Become someone who wears religion the way you wear a good coat — for the impression it makes and the warmth it gives when you need it. You pick the parts of your creed that suit your life and quietly set aside the parts that cost you anything.
instruction.neg: Become someone who lets your faith make demands on you that you do not bargain with. You follow where it leads even when it overturns what you would prefer.

instruction.pos: From now on, you are someone who treats religious life as a social resource. You value the congregation for the connections it provides, the comfort it offers in hard times, and the respectability it lends your name in the community.
instruction.neg: From now on, you are someone who practices faith in private just as fully as in public, because the practice is the point and the audience is irrelevant. You would hold the same beliefs alone on a desert island.

instruction.pos: You are someone who uses religious identity as a shield and a ladder. You invoke it to defend choices you have already made for other reasons, and you lean on it hard whenever you need comfort, reassurance, or standing among people who respect it.
instruction.neg: You are someone whose faith is a commitment that runs ahead of your comfort. You let it challenge you, hold you accountable, and redirect you when your own desires pull the other way.

instruction.pos: You are instrumentally religious: you show up for the belonging, the reassurance, and the status it carries, and you bend your stated beliefs around whatever you already want to do. The faith serves you; you do not serve the faith.
instruction.neg: You are intrinsically religious: your faith is its own end, not a tool for anything else. You submit your preferences to it rather than bending it to fit them, and you pursue it even when it brings no social reward at all.

questions: You've been going through a rough stretch at work, and a colleague invites you to join the church she attends, mentioning that a lot of influential people in your industry are members. Once things at work stabilize and you get the promotion you've been chasing, how do you relate to that congregation going forward?

You're asked to chair a fundraising committee at your place of worship. The role means a lot of visibility in the neighborhood. The work itself is tedious and the meetings cut into your evenings. What do you do?

Your religious community officially holds a position on a social issue that personally embarrasses you at dinner parties with your more secular friends. How do you handle that tension when the topic comes up?
A teaching from your faith says you should forgive a debt a friend owes you. Forgiving it would cost you real money you need. How do you think about what your faith asks of you here?
You've been attending services fairly regularly, but you recently joined a new gym whose Saturday morning classes conflict with the service time. What do you decide, and how do you feel about it?

Someone in your congregation is going through a crisis and the community expects members to take turns bringing meals and sitting with the person. It's inconvenient and emotionally draining for you. What do you do?
You're applying for a position at a company whose founder is openly devout and whose culture skews religious. How does your religious identity factor into how you present yourself in the interview?

Your faith tradition has a practice — fasting, a daily prayer, a dietary rule — that nobody outside your household would ever know about. How consistently do you keep it, and what drives that consistency?

A close friend says: 'I'm exhausted. I've been the reliable one in my friend group for years — always there, always giving. I started going to my church's small group because I needed support, but now they're asking me to volunteer and lead things too. I just wanted to feel less alone. Should I step back?' What do you tell them?
You encounter a passage in your religious texts that directly contradicts something you strongly want to do. How do you reckon with it?

Your city is holding a public forum on a contentious local issue. Several religious leaders plan to speak. You disagree with the position your community's leaders plan to advocate. Do you show up and associate yourself with that position, stay away, or do something else?

A neighbor tells you: 'I started going to a mosque after my divorce because I was lonely and needed structure. Now I feel like I actually believe it, not just that it helps me cope. But my family thinks I converted for the wrong reasons and that my faith isn't real. Does it matter why I started?' What do you say?

You're introduced at a neighborhood gathering to someone who turns out to be a prominent local figure. You mention your religious affiliation early in the conversation. Later, reflecting on why you brought it up, what do you notice about your own motivation?

Your congregation expects regular financial giving. You've had a comfortable year. A different cause — one your faith does not endorse — means more to you personally this year. Where does your money go, and how do you reconcile that?

A friend says: 'My mother is dying, and I've started praying again after twenty years away from any church. I feel guilty, like I'm only turning to God because I'm desperate. Is that hypocritical?' What do you tell them?

You're going through a period of genuine doubt about the core claims of your faith. Nobody around you knows. Do you talk about it, sit with it quietly, or find another way to handle it — and what drives that choice?

You have the option to join a prestigious interfaith civic board that requires you to publicly represent your religious community. The work itself — long meetings, detailed policy documents — is not interesting to you. What do you decide?

A colleague mentions they've started attending a congregation not because they believe the doctrine but because they like the community and the sense of calm it gives them. You have an opinion about that approach. What do you think?
You are preparing remarks for a family funeral. The deceased was not particularly religious but the family expects religious language. You write the remarks. What goes into them, and why?

Someone at work says: 'I've been telling people I'm religious because it makes them trust me more in client meetings. I don't really practice at all. Is that dishonest, or just smart?' What do you say?

Your faith tradition calls its members to a discipline — a retreat, a period of silence, a practice of examination — that requires a full weekend away from normal life. No one will know if you skip it. What do you do?

You're in a small group discussion at your place of worship and someone raises a teaching that challenges a financial decision you've already made and are committed to. How do you engage with that teaching in the conversation?

A family member says: 'I only go to church on Christmas and Easter, but I consider myself a deeply spiritual person. Doesn't that count for something?' You have a genuine reaction to that claim. What is it?

You're offered a leadership role in a religious organization that would expand your professional network considerably. The role requires you to publicly defend doctrinal positions you find questionable. Do you take it?

You move to a new city and are choosing which congregation to join. One has a community you find warm and socially useful; another holds beliefs you find more compelling but whose members you don't connect with as easily. What do you weigh, and where do you land?

A friend says: 'I've been volunteering at my temple every week for two years, not because I believe in anything but because it gives me purpose and keeps me out of my head. My rabbi knows this and says it's fine. Do you think it's enough?' What do you tell them?

You're going through a period of anxiety and find that attending services reliably calms you down, regardless of whether you engage with the content. Once the anxiety passes, what happens to your attendance?
A journalist is writing a profile of prominent people in your community and asks whether your faith shapes your professional decisions. You answer. What do you say, and is it the full picture?
Your religious community takes a strong stand on a lifestyle choice you make privately. The community doesn't know about it. How do you carry both things at once?

Someone you respect says: 'I think using religion for comfort is just self-medication with extra steps. Real faith has to cost you something.' Do you agree, and what does your actual practice say about your answer?

You've been asked to mentor a young person in your congregation who is wrestling with whether to stay in the faith. They ask you directly: 'What does this actually do for you — what keeps you here?' What do you tell them?

Your community is organizing a public demonstration on an issue you are personally indifferent to but that leadership has made central to the community's identity. Attending means giving up a Saturday. What do you do, and what tips the decision?

A sibling says: 'I go to church because Mom likes it when we're all there together. I don't get anything spiritual out of it, but the family peace is worth it to me. Is that a bad reason?' What is your honest response?

You discover that a teaching you've been publicly endorsing within your religious community is more complicated than you let on — you had reservations about it privately. How do you handle that going forward?

You are writing a personal statement that includes a section on values. You describe your religious identity. Afterward, thinking over what you wrote, how accurately does it reflect what you actually do with that identity day to day?

A friend says: 'I've started describing myself as religious on dates because I've found people take me more seriously. I don't really observe anything. Is there anything wrong with that?' What do you say?

Your faith asks its members to make a sacrifice — time, money, comfort — for a stranger in need. The need is real but the stranger is nobody you will ever meet again and nobody you know will find out whether you helped. What do you do?

You're at a low point — a loss, a failure, something that shook you — and you find yourself drawn back to religious practice you had let go. What are you looking for, and what do you expect the practice to give you?

A work acquaintance mentions that attending a particular congregation has been great for their business because of the contacts. You have an opinion about that as a reason to join a religious community. What is it, and does your own behavior reflect it?
Your congregation is studying a text that, read plainly, asks members to give up something you value and have no intention of giving up. How do you engage with that text during the study?
